newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Cholera threat delays UN Rwanda repatriation plan.
newsitem.headline: Cholera threat delays UN Rwanda repatriation plan.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency cited fears of a spread of cholera for its decision to delay the repatriation of tens of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees from Zaire that was due to start on Friday.

The rebel governor of Upper Zaire region had expressed concern that the programme could jeapordise the health of local residents so UNHCR would not go ahead with its original schedule, UNHCR regional spokesman Paul Stromberg said.
"The governor invoked health concerns, worrying that the operation might somehow propagate cholera," Stromberg told reporters.
"We are optimistic that they (regional authorities) will conclude that this is safe to do and that we will be able to start on Saturday," Stromberg said.
According to U.N. figures, 330 cholera cases and 19 cholera deaths have been recorded at Kasese refugee camp, 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani.
A total of 74 refugees died on Thursday and bodies lined the muddy track through Biaro camp where miserable Rwandans took shelter under plastic sheeting from torrential rains.
Around 100,000 sick and exhausted Rwandan refugees arrived near a railway line south of Zaire's third city Kisangani last month begging to go home after a five-month trek through the jungle.
More than a million Hutu refugees fled East Zaire camps last October and November at the start of a campaign by rebels against the government.

Most returned to Rwanda via Goma in November but hundreds of thousands more fled deeper into Zaire, among them members of the former Rwandan government army and extremist Interahamwe militia held responsible for massacres during the 1994 genocide.

Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire led by Laurent Kabila control more than half of Zaire in a six month campaign to oust ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko, Zaire's ruler since 1965.

U.N. agencies and non-governmental organisations are nursing the refugees back to health and UNHCR has devised a plan to take the refugees on trucks, planes and barges across the Zaire river back to Rwanda.
The airlift -- one of the biggest ever mounted -- could cost up to $50 million and involves three huge Ilyushin aircraft and a slightly smaller C-130.
Eighty healthy but unaccompanied Rwandan children were to be flown to the eastern town of Goma on Friday at the start of the operation.
Newly elected governor Yagi Sitolo told Reuters he opposed a Friday start for the plan because he feared cholera could spread if refugees are brought to Kisangani airport for the flight home.
The U.N. has played down the significance of the cholera outbreak, technically an epidemic.
Senior aid officials would meet regional authorities on Friday in an effort to convince them the repatriation posed no threat, Stromberg said.

Alliance military commanders say armed Hutu refugees pose a grave security threat and rebel government officials say U.N. money is being poured in for refugees when impoverished Zaireans should be the priority.
There is also a wider suspicion of foreign aid from Alliance and rebel government officials who stress self-reliance and argue western money sustained Mobutu.
Aid workers say they have started programmes to help local people and are flying home Zaireans displaced by the war.
